TO THE HONORABLE ADMINISTRATIVE LAW JUDGES:
This case asks whether Oncor and LCRA should receive permission to build the Bell County East to Big Hill transmission line, part of a larger route called Import Path 2. The Public Utility Commission sent two questions back to the administrative law judges (ALJs): Is the proposed transmission needed to meet reliability standards, and what congestion costs would it save consumers? Congestion occurs when limits on moving electricity prevent lower-cost power from reaching customers. The judges previously recommended denying the application in their Proposal for Decision (PFD). Applicants now seek a different result. This reply refers to Oncor and LCRA together as Applicants; to their Permian Basin Reliability Plan as the PBRP; to ERCOT, the Texas grid operator, by its usual name; and to its Regional Transmission Plans as RTPs.
Applicants have not cured the gaps in proof identified in the judges’ recommended decision. Their October 7 brief repeatedly relies on a larger grid plan without establishing why Import Path 2 is necessary. Applicants call Import Path 2 a reliability project and argue that they therefore need not demonstrate consumer congestion cost savings. That argument does not establish reliability need or supply the savings estimate requested in Issue 13. The judges should answer both questions directly: Applicants have not established that these facilities are necessary to meet reliability standards, and the cited evidence does not establish a separate estimate of consumer congestion cost savings attributable to them. The recommendation to deny the application should stand.
This reply answers Applicants’ October 7 brief and Commission Staff’s October 7 brief. It relies on evidence already admitted in this case. SOAH Order No. 35 requires pinpoint citations and does not allow new evidence. Citations use printed brief pages and exhibit page labels.
I. Applicants cannot shift their burden to landowners
The governing statute permits approval only upon a finding that the certificate is necessary for public service, accommodation, convenience, or safety. Applicants must prove the need for the facilities they want approved. Their response that no intervenor produced a study showing a reliable grid without Path 2 does not meet that burden. Landowners’ failure to fund a competing grid model is not proof of Applicants’ case.
Showing that three import paths work together does not, by itself, establish why Path 2 is necessary. Applicants must identify the reliability problem that requires Path 2 after accounting for the approved Paths 1 and 3. Their warning that removing Path 2 would jeopardize reliability must be supported by the admitted technical evidence. The absence of an opposing study does not fill a gap in Applicants’ proof.
The PFD already identified the central defect: regional tests of equipment failures under national reliability standards do not substitute for proof that Import Path 2 is needed. Applicants must answer that finding with evidence already admitted. Repeating that ERCOT recommended the larger plan does not resolve the defect.
The PFD gave four separate reasons for rejecting the claimed need: Applicants did not establish the need for Path 2 separately from the comprehensive three-path plan; projected demand did not establish its need; Applicants did not establish sufficient available generation at the eastern end to support the proposed westward transfers; and credible evidence showed that new and planned Permian Basin gas generation could reduce or eliminate the need. Applicants must answer those findings. Repeating that the larger plan was recommended does not answer them.
II. Including Path 2 in a model does not prove its necessity
Applicants call the later studies separate proof that the project is needed while acknowledging that the 2024 and 2025 planning models assume Path 2 is already in service. That is the gap in their argument. A model that includes a facility can show how the chosen system performs. Inclusion alone does not establish why that facility must be built.
The 2024 RTP expressly includes all three import paths in its 765-kV starting case. The 2025 RTP likewise includes the entire Texas 765-kV Strategic Transmission Expansion Plan (STEP) in its 2030 and 2031 starting cases, then reports no need to remove an element. Applicants cannot count each later inclusion as another independent demonstration without explaining the analysis that establishes Path 2’s necessity.
Applicants need to identify the year studied, the operating conditions, the safety rule the grid would fail, and how Path 2 fixes that failure. A study of the wider grid can supply that proof. Applicants have not answered the PFD’s concern by pointing to the absence of an alternative study paid for by landowners. The ALJs should decide whether the study results in evidence prove the project is needed, not presume necessity because Path 2 appears in the grid arrangement ERCOT chose to study.
Applicants cannot satisfy their burden for Import Path 2 simply by pointing to another transmission project. They must identify the evidence properly before these judges and explain what it proves about the facilities at issue here. Different utility ownership does not automatically exclude a study, and information about the connected grid may be relevant. But relevance to the larger system does not, by itself, establish the need for Path 2.
A factual assertion does not become evidence here merely because it appears in another docket. Findings must rest on evidence in the record or matters properly officially noticed, with an opportunity to contest official notice. The consolidation orders joined the need issues within Path 1 and within Path 2; they did not merge all five applications into one statewide application. The judges should respect the evidence properly before them in the consolidated Path 2 proceeding while requiring Applicants to establish its connection to these facilities.
For Issue 11, evidence that another import path is needed does not, by itself, establish that Import Path 2 is necessary to meet reliability standards. For Issue 13, savings attributed to several projects together do not, without a supported explanation, establish the estimated consumer congestion savings attributable to these facilities. The judges should disregard factual assertions drawn from other proceedings unless properly received into this record or officially noticed. For information properly before them, Applicants still must establish its connection to Import Path 2. A broader plan cannot fill a project-specific gap in proof merely because Applicants cite it.
Professional responsibility for the studies must be addressed
Applicants rely on technical studies, not just a general policy preference. Their October 7 brief says ERCOT performed reliability studies using national reliability standards and steady-state analysis to identify overloads, voltage instability, and power-flow failures. Their own admitted Exhibit JG-4 expressly includes a section titled “ERCOT Engineering Studies.” That section describes electrical-system studies used to demonstrate reliability and economics. Calling the resulting document a plan does not remove the engineering work behind it.
The professional-accountability concern is already in the admitted record. Tom Green, P.E., testified that the PBRP carries no Engineer of Record and that the proposed undertaking lacks a signed engineering document by a licensed engineer in responsible charge. His testimony calls for an answer. It does not itself establish a licensing violation, but Applicants cannot replace that answer with ERCOT’s name or the size of the regional plan.
Texas law covers engineering analysis, planning, and studies as well as construction drawings. If Applicants rely on a final engineering report subject to the sealing requirements, the required seal, signature, and professional responsibility must be addressed. A final planning report is not excused merely because construction drawings come later. Section 1001.402 also limits covered public officials’ acceptance of engineering documents within its scope. The Commission should address the requirements that apply to the work it is asked to rely upon.
The distinction is between gathering planning data and applying engineering judgment to recommend physical facilities. The Board’s transportation planning advisory recognizes that distinction, subject to statutory exemptions. Here, Applicants’ admitted Exhibit JG-4 describes electrical system reliability studies and comparisons of transmission alternatives. The ALJs should assess the work performed and its intended use when addressing professional responsibility. Calling a report a planning document does not answer that question.
The legal distinctions matter. Rule 137.33 distinguishes bound engineering reports requiring seals from other engineering work requiring professional identification, date, and signature. It also recognizes exemptions and certain public employee planning and review activities. The Act separately protects testimony and documents prepared solely for use as evidence. Any reliance on an exemption must identify the applicable provision and the facts supporting it; merely attaching a preexisting planning report to testimony does not establish that it was prepared solely for the hearing. Firm registration is a separate question under section 1001.405. Green’s testimony does not establish ERCOT’s registration status, and I do not ask the ALJs to assume an unproved violation.
If Applicants instead characterize the PBRP as only a preliminary or general planning document, that characterization does not make its recommendations conclusive proof that Path 2 is necessary. Applicants still must show what the admitted analysis establishes about these facilities. Under Issue 11, the questions remain: what reliability requirement would fail, under what conditions, and why is Path 2 necessary to correct it? Under Issue 13, neither a planning label nor an engineer’s seal supplies the missing estimate of consumer congestion savings attributable to Path 2. Professional authentication and proof of need are separate requirements; one cannot substitute for the other.
Either characterization leaves Applicants with work their brief has not done: address the professional responsibility applicable to the studies and establish what those studies actually prove about Path 2. A planning recommendation cannot carry more weight merely because the engineering behind it remains unexplained. The ALJs should weigh Green’s admitted testimony with the studies and retain the recommendation to deny for the failures of proof addressed in this reply.
III. Changing forecasts require evidence rather than assurances
ERCOT’s own reports describe changing demand, generation locations, and power-flow patterns. The 2024 RTP explains that imports to Central Texas and South Dallas shifted from the South Texas pattern identified in the 2023 RTP to a Coast Weather Zone pattern. The 2025 RTP describes further changes as large load growth outpaced generation growth. These changes make the assumptions decisive. Applicants must show which assumptions support Path 2 and what the results prove.
The reports measure demand in megawatts (MW) and gigawatts (GW); one gigawatt equals 1,000 megawatts. The 2025 RTP compares Far West load under 15 GW for 2029 in the 2023 RTP with nearly 19 GW for 2030 and nearly 20 GW for 2031 in the 2025 RTP. These are different planning years, but they show that the cases are not interchangeable. Applicants cannot present changing cases as repeated confirmation without explaining the effect of those changes on why this project is needed and when it is needed.
The need date also moved. Gurley acknowledges that the December 2024 sequencing spreadsheet listed 2038 as the year reliability need began to appear for all three import paths. He says the later evaluation established need by 2030. Moving the claimed need forward eight years requires a clear explanation backed by the study results. Changing the date does not prove the earlier deadline is necessary.
Applicants will rely on studies that tested lower demand. These are called sensitivity studies. The 2024 RTP reduced demand supported by utility officers’ letters from over 31 GW to less than 16 GW; the 2025 RTP reduced that category from over 23 GW to zero. Both also changed generation assumptions and reported similar key reliability needs. Those results show that the region can still need more transmission even when uncertain demand is removed. Applicants still must identify what those studies prove about the need for Path 2. A finding about the whole region is not an explanation of why this particular path is needed.
Gurley’s own rebuttal identifies the change in forecasting practice: HB 5066 requires consideration of loads without signed interconnection agreements. He also says ERCOT reduced forecasted loads in the 2024 RTP. Those points must be considered together. Including unsigned loads is permitted; their inclusion does not establish that every forecasted megawatt will materialize. Reducing a forecast likewise does not, by itself, prove Path 2 is necessary. Applicants must connect the admitted study results to these facilities. Landowners do not have to invalidate the entire PBRP to show that Applicants have failed to prove the need for Path 2.
The governing statute requires consideration of forecast growth and loads seeking interconnection, including customers that have not signed connection agreements. It does not require unquestioning acceptance. The PFD expressly rejected that reading. Forecasts must withstand scrutiny before they support this certificate.
IV. Applicants changing positions undermine the weight of their case
Applicants narrow the inquiry when resisting scrutiny and broaden it when seeking approval. The judges should confront that inconsistency directly. Applicants’ own filings show the positions described below. Their claims about the grid still need support from the evidence.
Applicants must give a consistent explanation of the project they seek to justify. They opposed discovery about the other import paths by calling those projects separate and distinct and disputing the relevance of their loading limits to need here. If Applicants rely on those paths’ combined performance to establish reliability or savings, they must explain that relationship and identify where landowners had a fair opportunity to test the supporting evidence. The chart compares Applicants’ litigation positions; it does not establish that every discovery objection was sustained or that a technical claim is true.
If the admitted evidence does not support the required findings, the applications should be denied. If Applicants need new factual evidence or materially different facilities to establish their case, they must pursue the applicable evidence, amendment, notice, and hearing procedures. Changed forecasts do not automatically require a new application, but missing proof cannot be supplied through new factual assertions in a brief after the record has closed. SOAH Order No. 35 expressly keeps this record closed and requires pinpoint citations. The ALJs should decide Issues 11 and 13 on that record.
Their sworn answers to written questions expose further gaps. Applicants did not know the total megawatts of Central Texas data-center demand in the forecast used to justify the Permian projects. Asked what percentage of large customer requests had been verified through site control, financial commitments, or signed agreements, Applicants gave no percentage. They also said the Rowan Project Temple partnership was not evaluated in the PBRP context.
Applicants answer that the grid is studied as one connected system, withdrawn loads are removed, and lower demand studies still show a need for the project. Those answers do not cure their inability to explain the load information identified above. Broad claims of confidence deserve less weight when the sponsoring parties cannot supply the requested underlying explanation. The judges should reject claims that go beyond what the evidence shows and hold Applicants to one consistent explanation.
V. Reliability warnings and other approvals do not cure the gap
Applicants invoke serious limits on power transfers in Far West Texas and the risk of cutting customers’ power to protect the grid. The cited exit strategy groups the import paths with other upgrades; Martin identifies six projects for the northern constraint and eight for the southern constraint, with the import paths described as critical elements. The analysis also accounts for about 2,500 megawatts of planned generation that can be turned up when needed. The seriousness of a regional problem does not relieve Applicants of establishing why these facilities are necessary to solve it.
Applicants’ answer that Path 2 can carry power in both directions does not resolve the generation question. The PFD identified no determination that Central Texas could serve its own data-center demand while supplying the proposed westward transfers. Bidirectional capability does not establish that sufficient generation will be available when those transfers are needed. Applicants must identify the admitted evidence answering that concern; describing another possible use for the line does not supply the missing analysis.
Approvals of Paths 1 and 3 support Applicants’ integrated-plan argument. They do not eliminate the Commission’s direction to answer Issues 11 and 13 in this proceeding. The judges’ updated recommended decision must explain how the evidence fixes the gaps they identified here. Importing another docket’s conclusion leaves that work unfinished.
Applicants’ proposed findings say they did not independently evaluate alternatives because the Commission approved the 765-kV option and directed the filing of applications. That procedural history does not itself prove necessity. Comparing 345-kV, 500-kV, and 765-kV plans addresses the choice among transmission options. Applicants still must explain how the admitted comparison establishes the need for Path 2. Permission to apply is not proof that the requested certificate should issue.
The rule that gives substantial weight to an ERCOT recommendation does not make approval automatic. The PFD expressly concluded that, even giving ERCOT’s recommendation substantial weight, the stronger credible evidence opposed accepting it for Path 2. Applicants must answer that separate finding. Reciting the great weight rule does not do so.
VI. Applicants have not supplied the Path 2 savings estimate
Issue 13 asks how much consumers would save if the proposed facilities reduced limits on moving electricity. Applicants respond that reliability projects need not demonstrate those savings, then cite benefits of a statewide network of major transmission lines. That claims an exemption and then offers numbers for a much larger plan. It supplies no separate dollar estimate of savings from Import Path 2 or the Bell County East to Big Hill facilities.
Applicants cite 1,443 miles of avoided upgrades, $890 million in avoided construction-outage costs, and more than $270 million in annual savings. Their source describes a network of 765-kilovolt transmission lines, not a calculation of Path 2’s share of the savings. Historical statewide and West Texas congestion costs likewise do not establish how much this project would save. A large statewide number does not tell us what this project would save.
The underlying comparison evaluates complete 345-kV and 765-kV plans for 2034 and 2039. It reports different measures: the cost of producing electricity, the amount consumers pay for energy, and a market measure of transmission constraints called congestion rent. The 765-kV plan has $136 million less consumer-energy-cost savings in 2034 than the 345-kV plan and approximately $229 million more in 2039. Its congestion rent is lower by $94 million and $172 million, respectively. Those are different measures and different years for whole-plan alternatives. None is identified as Path 2’s consumer congestion savings.
The report also states that large customer demand supported by utility officers’ letters was unavailable when the computer models for the cost comparison were prepared and was excluded from those base cases. Applicants cannot treat those economic assumptions and the reliability assumptions as interchangeable. For each number, Applicants must explain what it measures, what it is compared with, the year it covers, and the facilities it includes.
Staff repeats the reliability exemption and offers statewide comparisons as an alternative argument for approval based on savings. Staff’s support is not a substitute for proof. Its discussion supplies no Path 2 allocation. Consumers and affected landowners deserve an explanation of why these facilities are necessary and what the evidence establishes about their benefits and costs. Staff’s endorsement leaves those questions unanswered. The ALJs should reject Staff’s recommendation to the extent it rests on the same gaps in proof as Applicants’ case. If Applicants fail to establish reliability need, Staff’s endorsement does not establish an alternative basis for approval.
The ALJs should state the result plainly: the cited evidence does not establish a separate estimate of consumer congestion cost savings attributable to these facilities or Import Path 2. The amount is unestablished. Calling the project necessary for reliability would not create the missing estimate. An exemption from an economic approval test does not answer the question the Commission asked.
VII. Proposed Findings of Fact
I request the following findings, with numbering conformed to the updated recommended decision. Findings on what the reports say should remain separate from the ultimate finding on whether Applicants proved need.
1. The 2024 RTP’s 765-kV starting case included all three Permian Basin import paths. The 2025 RTP included the entire STEP in its 2030 and 2031 starting cases.
2. The 2024 and 2025 reduced-demand studies also changed generation assumptions and reported similar key regional reliability needs. Those results must be assessed according to the years, facilities and assumptions actually studied.
3. Gurley acknowledged that the December 2024 sequencing spreadsheet listed 2038 as the year reliability need began to appear for all three import paths. He testified that later evaluation established need in 2030. The claimed earlier need must be supported by the results of that evaluation.
4. The Far West operating-constraint evidence identifies multiple upgrades and treats the three import paths as a group. Martin describes the paths as critical elements of the broader solution.
5. Applicants’ statewide economic comparison evaluates whole 345-kV and 765-kV plans. Its production-cost, consumer-energy-cost and congestion-rent figures are different measures, not separate estimates assigned to Import Path 2.
6. The evidence cited in Applicants’ and Staff’s remand briefs does not establish a separate estimate of consumer congestion cost savings for these facilities or Import Path 2. The amount remains unestablished. This is not a finding that savings are zero.
7. After weighing the admitted studies, testimony, reduced-demand results and broader-plan evidence, Applicants have not established that these facilities are necessary to meet state or federal reliability standards. This is the ultimate factual finding requested on the arguments above.
8. Staff’s alternative economic argument relies on statewide comparisons. The cited discussion does not establish a Path 2 share of the benefits or demonstrate the required project comparison of benefits and consumer costs.
9. Applicants’ Exhibit JG-4 describes its analysis as “ERCOT Engineering Studies.” Green’s admitted direct testimony questions the PBRP’s Engineer of Record and signed professional accountability. That testimony raises a concern to be weighed; it is not a finding that ERCOT lacks registration or that a licensing violation has been established.
VIII. Proposed Conclusions of Law
1. A certificate may issue only upon the required finding that it is necessary for the service, accommodation, convenience or safety of the public. On the requested findings above, the application should be denied.
2. Forecast growth and customers seeking connection must be considered, including customers without signed connection agreements. That requirement does not compel acceptance of unsupported assumptions or remove the need for the required certificate finding.
3. Giving the required weight to a qualifying ERCOT recommendation does not make it conclusive. The decision must still assess the evidence supporting need for the proposed facilities.
4. A reliability project’s exemption from the economic-project approval tests does not itself supply an estimate of consumer congestion savings. The Commission’s remanded Issue 13 must be answered according to what the record establishes.
5. If the facilities are not shown necessary to meet state or federal reliability standards, Applicants must establish an applicable alternative basis for approval. Staff’s statewide benefits alone do not establish satisfaction of the economic-project criteria for these facilities.
6. Applicable professional-engineering requirements depend on the work, its authorship, and any established exemption. A seal or exemption does not establish reliability need or consumer congestion savings. Findings on Issues 11 and 13 must rest on what the admitted evidence proves about the proposed facilities.
IX. Prayer
For these reasons, I respectfully ask the ALJs to answer Issue 11 by finding that Applicants have not established that the proposed facilities are necessary to meet state or federal reliability standards; answer Issue 13 by finding that a separate estimate of consumer congestion savings for these facilities or Import Path 2 remains unestablished; adopt the requested findings and conclusions; and retain the recommendation to deny the application.
Applicants seek permission to burden private property and commit consumers to these facilities. They must prove their case. Repeating a regional recommendation, changing the assumptions, and citing statewide savings does not answer the missing project questions. The application must be denied.
Respectfully submitted,

Texas law covers engineering analysis, planning, and studies as well as construction
drawings. If Applicants rely on a final engineering report subject to the sealing
requirements, the required seal, signature, and professional responsibility must be
addressed. A final planning report is not excused merely because construction drawings
come later. Section 1001.402 also limits covered public officials' acceptance of
engineering documents within its scope. The Commission should address the
requirements that apply to the work it is asked to rely upon.17
The distinction is between gathering planning data and applying engineering judgment
to recommend physical facilities. The Board's transportation planning advisory
recognizes that distinction, subject to statutory exemptions. Here, Applicants' admitted
Exhibit JG-4 describes electrical system reliability studies and comparisons of
transmission alternatives. The ALJs should assess the work performed and its intended
use when addressing professional responsibility. Calling a report a planning document
does not answer that question.18
The legal distinctions matter. Rule 137.33 distinguishes bound engineering reports
requiring seals from other engineering work requiring professional identification, date,
and signature. It also recognizes exemptions and certain public employee planning and
review activities. The Act separately protects testimony and documents prepared solely
for use as evidence. Any reliance on an exemption must identify the applicable
provision and the facts supporting it; merely attaching a preexisting planning report to
testimony does not establish that it was prepared solely for the hearing. Firm
registration is a separate question under section 1001.405. Green's testimony does not
establish ERCOT's registration status, and I do not ask the ALJs to assume an
unproved violation.19

Ill. Changing forecasts require evidence rather than assurances
ERCOT's own reports describe changing demand, generation locations, and power-flow
patterns. The 2024 RTP explains that imports to Central Texas and South Dallas shifted
from the South Texas pattern identified in the 2023 RTP to a Coast Weather Zone
pattern. The 2025 RTP describes further changes as large load growth outpaced
generation growth.21 These changes make the assumptions decisive. Applicants must
show which assumptions support Path 2 and what the results prove.
The reports measure demand in megawatts (MW) and gigawatts (GW); one gigawatt
equals 1,000 megawatts. The 2025 RTP compares Far West load under 15 GW for
2029 in the 2023 RTP with nearly 19 GW for 2030 and nearly 20 GW for 2031 in the
2025 RTP. These are different planning years, but they show that the cases are not
interchangeable.22 Applicants cannot present changing cases as repeated confirmation
without explaining the effect of those changes on why this project is needed and when it
is needed.
The need date also moved. Gurley acknowledges that the December 2024 sequencing
spreadsheet listed 2038 as the year reliability need began to appear for all three import
paths. He says the later evaluation established need by 2030.23 Moving the claimed
need forward eight years requires a clear explanation backed by the study results.
Changing the date does not prove the earlier deadline is necessary.
Applicants will rely on studies that tested lower demand. These are called sensitivity
studies. The 2024 RTP reduced demand supported by utility officers' letters from over
31 GW to less than 16 GW; the 2025 RTP reduced that category from over 23 GW to
zero. Both also changed generation assumptions and reported similar key reliability
needs.24 Those results show that the region can still need more transmission even when
uncertain demand is removed. Applicants still must identify what those studies prove

Vlll. Proposed Conclusions of Law
1. A certificate may issue only upon the required finding that it is necessary for the
service, accommodation, convenience or safety of the public. On the requested findings
above, the application should be denied.58
2. Forecast growth and customers seeking connection must be considered, including
customers without signed connection agreements. That requirement does not compel
acceptance of unsupported assumptions or remove the need for the required certificate
finding.59

conclusive. The decision must still assess the evidence supporting need for the
proposed facilities.60

itself supply an estimate of consumer congestion savings. The Commission's remanded
Issue 13 must be answered according to what the record establishes.61
5. If the facilities are not shown necessary to meet state or federal reliability standards,
Applicants must establish an applicable alternative basis for approval. Staffs statewide
benefits alone do not establish satisfaction of the economic-project criteria for these
facilities.62
